findings.issue: Telnet session detected — full plaintext remote shell
findings.explanation: Telnet provides no encryption whatsoever. Every keystroke, including passwords and commands, is transmitted in cleartext. This is considered completely insecure for any production use.
findings.recommendation: Replace Telnet with SSH (port 22) immediately. Disable Telnet service on all devices.

findings.explanation: FTP sends credentials (USER/PASS commands) and file content in cleartext. Credentials are trivially sniffable on the same network segment.
findings.recommendation: Replace FTP with SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) or FTPS (FTP over TLS).

findings.issue: Sensitive keyword 'USER ' found in plaintext payload
findings.explanation: The payload contains the string 'USER ', suggesting that credentials or sensitive authentication data are being transmitted in plaintext. This data is fully readable by any network eavesdropper.
findings.recommendation: Ensure all authentication occurs over an encrypted channel (HTTPS, SFTP, SSH). Never transmit credentials in cleartext.

findings.issue: Trivial FTP (TFTP) detected — no authentication or encryption
findings.explanation: TFTP provides no authentication and no encryption. It is commonly used to serve firmware/config files on networks, making it a high-value attack target.
findings.recommendation: Use SFTP or SCP for secure file transfer. Restrict TFTP to isolated management VLANs.

findings.explanation: TLS 1.0 is deprecated (RFC 8996). Vulnerable to BEAST and POODLE-TLS attacks.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade to TLS 1.2 minimum. Prefer TLS 1.3.

findings.explanation: HTTP transmits data in plaintext, including cookies, form data, and credentials. Any network observer (ISP, attacker on LAN, proxy) can intercept and read or modify this traffic.
findings.recommendation: Migrate to HTTPS (TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3). Implement HSTS headers.

findings.explanation: POP3 on port 110 transmits email credentials and message content in cleartext. Attackers on the same network can harvest login credentials and read private email.
findings.recommendation: Use POP3S (port 995) with TLS, or migrate to IMAP over TLS (port 993).

findings.explanation: IMAP on port 143 without STARTTLS exposes email credentials and message content in plaintext. This allows credential theft and email eavesdropping.
findings.recommendation: Enforce STARTTLS on port 143, or use IMAPS on port 993.

findings.issue: SNMP v1/v2c likely — community strings in cleartext
findings.explanation: SNMP versions 1 and 2c use cleartext community strings as authentication. These strings can be intercepted and used to query or even configure network devices.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade to SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption (authPriv mode).

findings.explanation: TLS 1.1 is deprecated (RFC 8996). No longer considered secure.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade to TLS 1.2 minimum. Prefer TLS 1.3.

findings.explanation: SMTP on port 25 without STARTTLS transmits email in plaintext. While server-to-server SMTP is sometimes plaintext by design, it is best practice to enforce TLS.
findings.recommendation: Configure SMTP with STARTTLS (port 587) or SMTPS (port 465) for submission.

findings.issue: Unencrypted HTTP traffic on alternate port 8080
findings.explanation: Port 8080 is commonly used as an HTTP proxy or alternate web server port. Traffic on this port is typically unencrypted.
findings.recommendation: Use HTTPS on port 443 or 8443 instead.

findings.explanation: Traditional syslog over UDP port 514 transmits log data in cleartext with no integrity protection. Logs can be intercepted or spoofed.
findings.recommendation: Use Syslog over TLS (RFC 5425) on TCP port 6514.
